planting.note: Direct sow fresh seed onto bare, thin soil in fall so winter cold and moisture break dormancy; this diminutive prairie plant cannot compete with thatch or taller vegetation, so choose a lean upland site with little competing growth.

directions: Prairie buttercup is one of the earliest wildflowers to bloom on dry upland and hill prairies of the glaciated till plains, pushing up a low rosette of softly hairy, lobed leaves and small glossy yellow five-petaled flowers while most other prairie forbs are still dormant. By early summer the foliage withers away entirely and the plant disappears underground until the following spring, so it is best combined with later-emerging neighbors that can fill the same space. It thrives in thin, lean, well-drained soil where taller vegetation and leaf litter are sparse, conditions that mimic the eroded hill prairies and gravelly till-plain remnants it naturally occupies. Once established it needs no care beyond leaving its summer dormancy undisturbed.

planting.note: Scatter seed directly onto open soil among the roots of an established native grass stand once frost danger passes, since this hemi-parasite needs contact with living grass roots to thrive and struggles if sown into bare, grass-free ground.

directions: Slenderleaf false foxglove is a wiry, branching native annual found scattered through till-plain prairie remnants and moist meadows from Ohio through Indiana and Illinois, where its narrow leaves and thin stems are easy to overlook until its small pink to lavender, bell-shaped flowers open from late summer into fall. Each flower lasts only a single day but is quickly replaced by others along the branching stems, drawing small native bees throughout its bloom period. As a hemiparasite it taps into the roots of nearby prairie grasses for part of its nutrition, so it performs best interplanted among little bluestem or other established warm-season grasses rather than grown alone in open soil. It behaves as a true annual, reseeding itself each year wherever its grass hosts persist.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall for natural cold stratification, or plant divisions in spring, into moist to average, well-drained prairie soil in full sun; prairie sundrops spreads by shallow rhizomes, so give it room among equally vigorous mesic-prairie neighbors.

directions: Unlike most evening primroses, prairie sundrops opens its clear yellow, four-petaled flowers by day rather than at dusk, brightening wet-mesic to mesic tallgrass prairie remnants of the glaciated till plains of Ohio, Indiana, and Illinois from late spring into midsummer. The clump spreads gradually by shallow rhizomes into a loose colony rather than staying as a single tidy crown, so it mixes naturally with other assertive prairie companions rather than a refined border setting. Its day-opening flowers draw a range of day-flying native bees before giving way to narrow seed capsules later in the season. Established plantings tolerate average garden moisture but flower most heavily where soil stays evenly moist through the growing season.

planting.note: Direct sow in fall onto thin, lean, well-drained prairie soil in full sun, since this deep-rooted dry-prairie specialist resents rich, moist garden conditions and does best left undisturbed once established.

directions: Long-bearded hawkweed is a true dry-prairie specialist set apart from the shade-tolerant woodland hawkweeds by the dense, long, bristly hairs covering its stems and leaves, the feature behind both its common name and its distinctly shaggy look. From a basal rosette it sends up a tall, nearly leafless flowering stalk topped with a loose, branched cluster of small, dandelion-like yellow flower heads in mid- to late summer, well after most spring prairie forbs have finished blooming. It favors the lean, well-drained soils of dry hill prairies and glaciated till-plain remnants where competition from lusher vegetation is limited, and rarely persists on rich or disturbed ground. Its deep taproot makes established plants drought tolerant and essentially self-sufficient, with the late-season flowers drawing small native bees and other visiting insects.
